description: We are a team of three people with backgrounds in geospatial analysis, programming, and engineering.
summary:
Our project is an interactive app for exploring potential lunar landing sites and comparing the conditions they may face. Using NASA’s LOLA lunar elevation data and JPL’s DE440s data on the motion of the Moon and Earth it shows how terrain and changing celestial positions affect what a site can see. 

Users can choose two sites by entering their locations or selecting them on the Moon, then compare local terrain horizons, sunlight and Earth visibility, and estimated solar-panel output over time. The app helps scientists and planners identify promising locations, understand when terrain may block sunlight or the Earth, and begin assessing whether solar power could support lunar activity.
details:
What does it do?

Our project lets users explore and compare two potential lunar sites. For each site, it shows how the surrounding terrain may affect visibility of the Sun and Earth, and estimates the solar energy a panel could produce over time. Users can select sites by entering coordinates or clicking on the Moon, adjust solar panel settings, compare plots, and create scientific datasets and download them. The data our app generates is:

1. Sun azimuth
2. Sun elevation
3. Sun horizon (terrain elevation at Sun's azimuth)
4. Sun disc visibility ([0 - 1])
5. Earth azimuth
6. Earth elevation
7. Earth horizon (terrain elevation at Earth's azimuth)
8. Earth disc visibility (0/1)
9. Power
10. Irradiance
11. Panel - Sun incidence
12. Energy produced (kWh)

How does it work?

The app combines NASA LOLA elevation data with JPL DE440s information about the changing positions of the Moon and Earth around the Sun. It uses the terrain around each selected site to estimate the local horizon, then shows when terrain may obstruct the Sun or Earth. As users move through simulated time, they can see how visibility and estimated panel output change.

For manageable storage and computation, the app uses NASA’s LOLA LDEM_64 terrain dataset rather than the denser LDEM_256 or LDEM_512 datasets. For the same reasons the JPL DE440 orbital positions and lunar orientations are subsampled at daily intervals and interpolated between samples.

To assess Sun/Earth visibility a horizon profile is built for each site at the moment of the site's selection. The app samples terrain along a circle around the site using a discrete step and records the highest terrain angle in each direction to build a skyline. For the Sun, the app checks many points across its disc against the skyline and reports the visible fraction from 0 to 1. For Earth, it checks whether any part of its disc clears the skyline, reporting 1 if visible and 0 if not.

Panel power is calculated using a simple solar panel model, where A is the solar panel surface, eta is the solar panel efficiency, I1 is the reference sunlight intensity at one AU (configured as 1361 W/m²), d is the site to Sun distance, n * s is the incidence (the cosine of the angle between the unit directions pointing straight out from the panel, and from the panel toward the Sun) and f_sun is the percentage of the sun disc that is visible.






What benefits does it have?

It brings terrain, location, visibility, and solar-energy estimates together in one interactive view. Comparing two sites can help users quickly spot differences in sunlight and potential power generation, explore how those conditions vary over time, and prepare data for further analysis. It provides a friendly and targeted UI that enables rapid set up of the simulation and generation of the desired scientific data.

What do you hope to achieve?

The project aims to make early lunar-site exploration easier to understand and discuss. It provides a way to rapidly identify promising locations and questions for deeper study, by generating scientifically accurate data that can be used for further analysis.
